title: The Normal Approximation to the Binomial
short: Approximate Binomial(n, p) with a normal curve, widening each whole number to an interval of width 1: P(X ≤ 12) ≈ P(Y < 12.5).
trouble: Students skip the continuity correction, or move the boundary the wrong way: P(X < 12) = P(X ≤ 11) ≈ P(Y < 11.5).

blocks.html: A binomial count is a sum of independent 0–1 trials, so by the central limit theorem it is close to normal when $n$ is large. But the binomial lives on whole numbers and the normal curve on all real numbers. The continuity correction bridges the two.

For $X$ binomial with $np(1 - p)$ reasonably large (say at least 10), use $Y$ normal with mean $np$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$, and widen each whole number $k$ to $[k - 0.5,\ k + 0.5]$: $$P(X \le k) \approx P(Y < k + 0.5), \qquad P(X \ge k) \approx P(Y > k - 0.5), \qquad P(X = k) \approx P(k - 0.5 < Y < k + 0.5).$$

Draw the binomial pmf as bars of width 1, centered on the whole numbers. The bar for $k$ covers $[k - 0.5, k + 0.5]$ and its area is $P(X = k)$. The normal curve approximates the tops of the bars, so the area under the curve over the same stretch approximates the same probability. For $X \le k$ the bars run through the one at $k$, which ends at $k + 0.5$. Without the correction, a single value would get probability 0, and each "$\le$" question would lose half a bar.

blocks.cap: The normal curve for 100 fair coin flips: the area to the left of 45.5 approximates the chance of at most 45 heads.

blocks.title: At most 45 heads
blocks.q: Flip a fair coin 100 times. Approximate $P(X \le 45)$. Use $\Phi(-0.9) = 0.1841$.
steps: $\approx 0.1841$. The exact binomial value is $0.1841$ too.

blocks.html: Skipping the correction, or moving the boundary the wrong way. $P(X < 12)$ is $P(X \le 11)$, so the boundary is $11.5$, not $12.5$. Check: list which whole numbers the event includes, and make the normal interval run half a unit beyond the extreme ones.
